mainTopic: Buying goods that may be stolen, the seriousness of robbery, and which craftsmen's leftovers belong to them
overview: The amud opens by concluding that רבי יהודה's words about buying animals are a leniency. Next comes the משנה's ban on buying from שומרי פירות: רבא explains that an אריס is different, because he owns a share of the crop, and a ברייתא allows buying from watchmen who sell openly. רב and שמואל then argue about when you may buy from a known גזלן, and רב יהודה rules like שמואל. The גמרא discusses the property of a מסור, tells how רב חסדא dismissed his sharecropper, and brings פסוקים teaching that robbery is like taking a life. רבי יוחנן says that robbing even a פרוטה is like killing, and that this includes harming the victim's children, taking by force while paying, and indirect harm, as with שאול and the גבעונים. A ברייתא lists what may be bought from women, olive pressers and others, and what charity collectors may accept. רבינא accepts jewelry in wealthy מחוזא because there it counts as small. Finally, a new משנה rules on which leftover threads and shavings belong to the craftsman and which belong to the owner, and the גמרא begins with a ברייתא about the launderer.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's statement is a leniency on the latter clause
steps.stepSummary: Because רבי יהודה said 'in every place,' the גמרא concludes that he is talking about the later clause and is being lenient. The גמרא accepts this.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he said 'in every place,' this shows he is talking about the later part, and he means it as a leniency. Yes, that is the conclusion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the earlier question about רבי יהודה. His words 'in every place' prove that he is adding a leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, it was unclear whether רבי יהודה was being strict or lenient. The words 'in every place' only make sense as permission to buy a few animals anywhere. So his statement goes on the later clause and is lenient.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it / conclude from this
The later clause of a teaching

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה's ruling is a leniency. The words 'in every place' prove it.

phrases.english: From the fact that he said "in every place,"
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהודה, who allowed buying four or five animals anywhere.

phrases.english: conclude from it that he is referring to the latter clause, and as a leniency!
Conclude from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the discussion from the previous daf about how to read רבי יהודה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: רבי יהודה's statement refers to the later clause and is lenient.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה about produce watchmen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next part of the משנה: you may not buy from people who guard produce.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And not from produce watchmen,' and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next line of the משנה to start a new topic. This sets up the story about רבא that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה forbids buying wood and fruit from watchmen. They do not own the produce, so what they sell may be stolen from the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: Watchmen who guard someone else's produce
Etc.; the rest of the quote

phrases.english: "And not from produce watchmen," etc.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You may not buy produce or wood from produce watchmen.

steps.title: רבא buys vine branches from a sharecropper
steps.stepSummary: רבא bought grapevine branches from an אריס.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא bought vine branches from a sharecropper.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about what רבא did. This sets up אביי's challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An אריס works someone else's field for a share of the crop. Like a watchman, he is not the full owner. So the question is whether the משנה's rule applies to him too.

keyTerms.meaning: Sharecropper who works a field for a share of the crop

phrases.english: Rava purchased grapevine branches from a sharecropper.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real case that tests the משנה's rule.

steps.title: אביי challenges רבא from the משנה
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks how רבא could buy, since the משנה forbids buying wood and fruit from watchmen.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: But we learned, 'and not from produce watchmen, wood and fruit'!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges רבא's purchase using the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי treats an אריס like a watchman, since neither one fully owns the produce. If buying from a watchman is forbidden, buying from an אריס should be forbidden too.

keyTerms.meaning: But didn't we learn (in a משנה)?

phrases.english: Abaye said to him:
But didn't we learn:
"And not from produce watchmen: wood and produce"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's action from step 3, using the משנה from step 2.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: An אריס is like a watchman, so the משנה's ban should apply to him.

steps.title: A sharecropper owns a share of the land, unlike a watchman
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the ban only covers a watchman, who owns nothing in the land. An אריס has a share, so we can assume he is selling his own part.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: That rule is about a watchman, who owns nothing at all in the land itself. But a sharecropper has a share in it, so say he is selling from his own part.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends his purchase by showing that an אריס is different from a watchman.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Watchmen are suspect because nothing they sell belongs to them. An אריס owns part of the crop, so it is reasonable to assume he is selling his own share. That doubt is enough to allow buying from him.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply only to (this case)

steps.whatToRemember: An אריס is different from a שומר. Because he owns a share, we may buy from him.
steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying watchmen are now allowed. The ban on buying from watchmen stays; an אריס is simply a different case.

phrases.english: He said to him: This applies to a watchman,
who has nothing at all in the land itself;
but a sharecropper, who does have a share in it,
say he is selling from his own share.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An אריס is just like a watchman and is forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: An אריס owns a share, so we assume he sells his own produce, and buying from him is allowed.

steps.title: ברייתא: buying from watchmen openly versus secretly
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says you may buy from watchmen when they sell openly, with baskets and scales in front of them. If they say 'hide it,' or sell from the back of the garden, buying is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: produce watchmen, you may buy from them when they sit and sell with baskets and scales in front of them. Any case where they say 'hide it' is forbidden. You may buy from them at the garden entrance, but not behind the garden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains when buying from watchmen is allowed after all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's ban covers a suspicious sale. Selling openly, with full equipment and at the entrance, suggests the owner allowed it. Secrecy, like 'hide it' or selling out back, points to theft.
steps.whatToRemember: An open, public sale is allowed. A secret sale is forbidden.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a practical test for spotting stolen goods: how openly is the item being sold?

phrases.english: The Sages taught: Produce watchmen:
one may buy from them when they are sitting and selling,
and the baskets are before them, and the scales are before them.
And in all cases where they said "Hide it," it is forbidden.
One may buy from them at the entrance of the garden,
but not from the back of the garden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא that sets limits on the משנה's ban on watchmen.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You may buy from watchmen who sell openly, but not when they sell secretly.

steps.title: When may one buy from a robber?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new question: from what point is it allowed to buy from a known גזלן?
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: A robber, from when is it permitted to buy from him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic about buying from a known robber. This sets up the מחלוקת in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far the cases involved only suspicion. Now the seller is known to steal. The question is how much of his property must be honestly his before we may buy from him.

keyTerms.meaning: It was stated (introduces an argument between אמוראים)

phrases.english: It was stated: A robber,
from when is it permitted to buy from him?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיתְּמַר גַּזְלָן מֵאֵימַת מוּתָּר לִקְנוֹת הֵימֶנּוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from suspected theft to a known robber.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How much of a robber's property must be his own before buying from him is allowed.

steps.title: רב: majority; שמואל: even a minority
steps.stepSummary: רב says you may buy only once most of the robber's property is his own. שמואל says even if only a small part is his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Not until most of it is his own. שמואל said: Even if only a minority is his own.
steps.whatsHappening: רב and שמואל give two different answers to the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב follows the majority: unless most of the property is honest, assume any item is stolen. שמואל is more lenient: as long as some of it is his own, this item might be one of those.
steps.whatToRemember: רב requires a majority of honest property. שמואל allows buying even when only a minority is honest.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אָמַר: עַד שֶׁתְּהֵא רוֹב מִשֶּׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: Rav says: Until the majority is from his own,
phrases.notes: He means it is forbidden until most of the robber's things are honestly his.

phrases.english: and Shmuel says: Even if a minority is his own.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר עַד שֶׁתְּהֵא רוֹב מִשֶּׁלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from step 7 with two opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: only when the majority is his own. שמואל: even when only a minority is his own.

steps.title: רב יהודה rules like שמואל in practice
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה told his attendant אדא to follow the lenient view of שמואל: you may buy from a known robber even if only a small part of his property is his own.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה instructed אדא his attendant according to the one who says: even if only a minority is his own.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows which side of the רב/שמואל argument was actually followed. רב יהודה gave a practical ruling like שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 8, רב needed most of the robber's property to be his own, while שמואל needed only a small part. Here a real ruling is reported, and it follows שמואל's lenient view. This tells us how the argument was settled in practice.

keyTerms.meaning: He instructed him (gave him a practical ruling)

steps.whatToRemember: In practice, רב יהודה ruled like שמואל: buying from a known robber is allowed even if only a small part of his property is his own.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda instructed
Adda the attendant
according to the words of the one who says
even a minority is his own.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles in practice the רב/שמואל argument from step 8.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The practical ruling follows שמואל: you may buy from a known robber even if only a minority of his property is his own.

steps.title: Argument: may you destroy an informer's property?
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא and רב יהודה argue about the property of a מסור. One says you may destroy it with your own hands; the other says you may not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The property of an informer: רב הונא and רב יהודה argue. One says it is permitted to destroy it directly, and one says it is forbidden to destroy it directly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: the property of a מסור. It reports an argument without yet saying who holds which view or why.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A מסור endangers other Jews' property by reporting it to non-Jewish authorities. The question is whether his own property loses its protection, so that someone may actively wreck it. The גמרא does not tell us which of the two אמוראים holds which view.

keyTerms.meaning: To destroy it with one's own hands (actively)

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא says 'one says... and one says' on purpose. It does not tell us whether רב הונא or רב יהודה is the lenient one.

phrases.english: The property of an informer:
Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda argue;
one says: it is permitted to destroy it directly,
and one says: it is forbidden to destroy it directly.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָמוֹן מָסוֹר רַב הוּנָא וְרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from buying from a robber to a related topic: the property of a wrongdoer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is an argument over whether a מסור's property may be actively destroyed.

steps.title: The reasons behind each side
steps.stepSummary: The lenient side says a מסור's property should not be treated more strictly than his body. The strict side says he may have good children who will inherit it, as the פסוק says the righteous will wear what the wicked prepared.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who permits destroying it reasons: his property should not be stricter than his body. The one who forbids reasons: perhaps he will have good offspring, and it is written: 'The wicked may prepare it, but the righteous shall wear it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reason behind each opinion from the previous step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lenient view uses a 'how much more so' type of logic: if the מסור himself may be harmed, his property cannot be more protected than he is. The strict view looks to the future: the money may end up with his righteous children, so destroying it hurts them. The פסוק from איוב backs this up: what the wicked gathers can end up with the righteous.

keyTerms.meaning: More strictly protected than his body
The wicked prepares, and the righteous wears

steps.whyThisMatters: The two reasons show two ways of looking at the property: as part of the wrongdoer himself, or as something that may later belong to innocent heirs.

phrases.english: The one who says it is permitted to destroy it directly:
his property should not be stricter than his body.
phrases.notes: Harming the מסור himself is allowed, so his property cannot have more protection than he does.

phrases.english: And the one who says it is forbidden to destroy it:
perhaps he will have good offspring,
and it is written: "The wicked may prepare it, but the righteous shall wear it."
phrases.notes: איוב 27:17

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for each side of the argument in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Lenient: property is not stricter than the body. Strict: the property may go to righteous heirs.

steps.title: רב חסדא dismisses his sharecropper
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא had a sharecropper who weighed out רב חסדא's share and weighed out his own share. רב חסדא dismissed him and quoted the פסוק: 'The wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא had a certain sharecropper who would weigh and give, weigh and take. He dismissed him and read upon himself: 'And the wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about רב חסדא and his אריס, ending with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sharecropper weighed out both shares himself. רב חסדא dismissed him and quoted a פסוק that calls such a person a 'sinner' (חוטא), whose wealth ends up with the righteous. So רב חסדא saw him as a wrongdoer, and the story ties back to the theme of a sinner's property reaching the righteous, the same idea as the פסוק in the previous step.

keyTerms.meaning: Sharecropper who works a field for a share of the crop
He applied a פסוק to himself

phrases.english: Rav Chisda had
a certain sharecropper,
who would weigh and give,
phrases.notes: He weighed out רב חסדא's portion and handed it over.

phrases.english: weigh and take.
He dismissed him,
and read regarding himself:
"And the wealth of the sinner is stored up for the righteous."
phrases.notes: משלי 13:22

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא הֲוָה לֵיהּ הָהוּא אֲרִיסָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of a sinner's wealth reaching the righteous, echoing the פסוק in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב חסדא dismissed his sharecropper and applied the פסוק about a sinner's wealth being stored up for the righteous.

steps.title: Whose soul does God take: the robbed or the robber?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a פסוק in איוב about the hope of the wicked. רב הונא and רב חסדא argue whether 'his soul' means the soul of the person who was robbed or the soul of the robber.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'For what is the hope of the godless, though he profits, when God takes away his soul?' רב הונא and רב חסדא argue about this. One says it means the soul of the robbed person. The other says it means the soul of the robber.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: a פסוק about robbers, and a dispute over who 'his soul' refers to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'his soul' could point to either person in the story. One view says robbing someone's money is like taking his very life. The other view says the robber will pay for his crime with his own life.

keyTerms.meaning: A wicked, godless person (here, the robber)

phrases.english: "For what is the hope of the godless, though he profits,
when God takes away his soul?"
phrases.notes: איוב 27:8

phrases.english: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda disagree about this:
One says: it means the soul of the robbed person,
and one says: it means the soul of the robber.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא וְרַב חִסְדָּא; חַד אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of פסוקים about robbers and the wicked, after רב חסדא's פסוק in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a dispute whether 'his soul' in איוב 27:8 is the victim's soul or the robber's soul.

steps.title: Source for the view that it is the victim's soul
steps.stepSummary: The view that it means the robbed person's soul brings a פסוק from משלי: greed 'takes the life of its owners.'
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says it means the soul of the robbed person learns it from the פסוק: 'So are the ways of everyone greedy for gain; it takes the life of its owners.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind the first view, using a פסוק from משלי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Its owners' sounds like the real owners of the money, meaning the victims. So the פסוק teaches that stealing someone's property is like taking his life. That supports reading 'his soul' in איוב as the victim's soul.

keyTerms.meaning: One who is greedy for dishonest gain

phrases.english: The one who says it is the soul of the robbed person:
because it is written: "So are the ways of everyone greedy for gain;
it takes the life of its owners."
phrases.notes: משלי 1:19

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל נִגְזָל – דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the first opinion in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: The view that 'his soul' in איוב means the victim's soul.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי 1:19: 'it takes the life of its owners.'

steps.title: Source for the view that it is the robber's soul
steps.stepSummary: The view that it means the robber's soul brings a פסוק from משלי: God will take the life of those who rob the poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who says it means the soul of the robber learns it from the פסוק: 'Do not rob the poor because he is poor, and do not crush the needy at the gate. For ה׳ will fight their fight, and will take the life of those who rob them.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind the second view, using a different פסוק from משלי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק clearly says God takes the life of the robbers. So the second view reads 'his soul' in איוב the same way: the robber pays with his own life.

keyTerms.meaning: And He will rob, take away

phrases.english: The one who says it is the soul of the robber:

phrases.aramaic: דִּכְתִיב: ״אַל תִּגְזׇל דַּל כִּי דַּל הוּא,
phrases.english: because it is written: "Do not rob the poor because he is poor,
and do not crush the needy at the gate.
For ה׳ will fight their fight,
and will take the life of those who rob them."
phrases.notes: משלי 22:22–23. The word קבע here means to rob.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאן דְּאָמַר נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁל גַּזְלָן – דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the second opinion in step 13, in parallel to step 14.
steps.raayaObject: The view that 'his soul' in איוב means the robber's soul.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי 22:22–23: 'and will take the life of those who rob them.'

steps.title: Challenge to the robber's-soul view from the first פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the robber's-soul view: what about the פסוק 'it takes the life of its owners,' which sounds like the victim?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other view too: isn't it written, 'it takes the life of its owners'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the second view with the first view's פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Its owners' seems to mean the true owners, the victims. If so, the robbed person's life is taken, which goes against the view that only the robber's soul is meant.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the other opinion)

phrases.english: And the other one too,
phrases.notes: 'The other one' here is the view that it means the robber's soul.

phrases.english: isn't it written: "it takes the life of its owners"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the first view's פסוק (step 14) against the second view (step 15).
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that 'his soul' means the robber's soul.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Its owners' sounds like the victims, so the פסוק seems to say the victim's life is taken.

steps.title: 'Its owners' means the current owner: the robber
steps.stepSummary: The robber's-soul view answers that 'its owners' means whoever owns the stolen item now, which is the robber.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'its owners' mean? Its current owners.
steps.whatsHappening: The second view explains the challenging פסוק so that it fits its own reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After the robbery, the robber holds the stolen item, so he is its 'owner' right now. So the פסוק really says greed takes the robber's life, and it supports this view instead of challenging it.

phrases.english: What does "its owners" mean?
Its current owners.
phrases.notes: He means the robber, who has the stolen item in his hands now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Its owners' means the original owners, the victims.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Its owners' means the current holder of the stolen item, the robber.

steps.title: Challenge to the victim's-soul view from the second פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the victim's-soul view: what about the פסוק 'and will take the life of those who rob them,' which is about the robbers?
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other view too: isn't it written, 'and will take the life of those who rob them'?
steps.whatsHappening: Now the גמרא does the same thing in reverse: it challenges the first view with the second view's פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק plainly says God takes the life of the robbers. That seems to go against the view that 'his soul' means the victim's soul.

phrases.english: And the other one too,
phrases.notes: This time 'the other one' is the view that it means the victim's soul.

phrases.english: isn't it written: "and will take the life of those who rob them"!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ נָמֵי, הָכְתִיב: ״וְקָבַע אֶת קֹבְעֵיהֶם נָפֶשׁ״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors step 16: turns the second view's פסוק (step 15) against the first view (step 14).
steps.kashyaTarget: The view that 'his soul' means the victim's soul.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק says the robbers' life is taken, which seems to back the opposite view.

steps.title: The פסוק is giving a reason: they robbed a soul
steps.stepSummary: The victim's-soul view answers that the end of the פסוק explains why God punishes the robbers: because they took the soul of their victims.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק is saying 'what is the reason.' What is the reason that God will rob those who rob them? Because they robbed a soul.
steps.whatsHappening: The first view explains the challenging פסוק so that it fits its own reading, and closes the discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'נפש' is read as the reason for the punishment, not as the punishment itself. God punishes the robbers because they robbed the victim's soul. So this פסוק also shows that robbery takes the victim's life, which supports the first view.

keyTerms.meaning: It is saying 'what is the reason' (the words give a reason)

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree on all the פסוקים; they only read them differently. One side says robbery takes the victim's life. The other says the robber will pay with his own life. Each side explains the other's פסוק to fit its own view.

phrases.english: It is saying "what is the reason":
What is the reason "He will rob those who rob them"?
Because they robbed a soul.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the structure of the פסוק as a cause and its reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: נפש is what God takes from the robbers.
steps.terutzMaskana: נפש is the reason God punishes them: they robbed the victim's soul.

steps.title: Robbing even a פרוטה is like taking a life
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that whoever robs his fellow of even a פרוטה's worth is considered as if he took his soul. He proves it from the פסוק in משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: anyone who robs his friend of something worth even a פרוטה, it is as if he took his soul from him. As the verse says: 'So are the ways of everyone greedy for gain; it takes the life of its owners.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן makes a strong statement: stealing even a tiny amount is like taking a person's life. He backs it up with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A פרוטה is the smallest amount of money that matters in הלכה, so רבי יוחנן means that even the smallest robbery counts. The פסוק says greed 'takes the life of its owners.' This is the same פסוק the גמרא just discussed in steps 16-17.

keyTerms.meaning: Robs, takes something openly by force
Worth a פרוטה, the smallest amount that counts in הלכה
One who is greedy for gain

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the tone for the end of the פרק. Robbery is not only a money issue; the גמרא treats it as close to taking a life.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan says:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַגּוֹזֵל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה –
phrases.english: Anyone who robs his fellow of something worth a perutah
it is as if he takes his soul from him,
as it is said:
"So are the ways of everyone greedy for gain,
it takes the life of its owners."
phrases.notes: משלי 1:19. This is the same פסוק the גמרא was just discussing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל הַגּוֹזֵל אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ שָׁוֶה פְּרוּטָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching. It uses a פסוק that was just discussed in steps 16-17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Robbing even a פרוטה is considered like taking the victim's life.

steps.title: Three more פסוקים showing robbery is like killing
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן adds three more פסוקים, each introduced with 'and it says'. One is from ירמיהו, one from יואל, and one about שאול and the גבעונים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it says: 'They will eat your harvest and your bread, your sons and your daughters.' And it says: 'For the violence of the children of יהודה, who shed innocent blood in their land.' And it says: 'It is for שאול and for his house of blood, because he killed the גבעונים.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן brings three more פסוקים to support his statement. Each one links taking someone's things to taking a life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק already proved the point, so these extra פסוקים look unnecessary. The גמרא will ask about this next. Each פסוק is going to teach a new detail.

keyTerms.meaning: And it says, introducing another פסוק
The גבעונים, a nation that made a treaty with ישראל

phrases.english: And it says:
"And they will eat your harvest and your bread,
your sons and your daughters."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 5:17

phrases.english: And it says:
"For the violence of the children of Judah,
who shed innocent blood in their land";
phrases.notes: יואל 4:19

phrases.english: And it says:
"It is for Shaul and for his house of blood,
because he killed the Givonim."
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 21:1

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more sources to רבי יוחנן's statement.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim that robbery is like taking a life

steps.title: Why bring so many פסוקים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what each extra 'and it says' adds, since the first פסוק already proved the point.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the point of 'and it says'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יוחנן needed more than one פסוק. This question sets up the next steps, which explain each extra פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that the גמרא does not bring extra sources for no reason. So each new פסוק must teach something the earlier one did not.

keyTerms.meaning: What, what is the point of

phrases.english: What is the point of "and it says"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions why step 21's extra פסוקים are needed.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What each extra פסוק adds beyond the first one

steps.title: The second פסוק: the robber harms the children too
steps.stepSummary: Without the second פסוק, we might think the robber takes only the victim's own life. The פסוק about 'sons and daughters' shows that he also harms the victim's children.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: only his own life is taken, but not the life of his sons and daughters. Come and hear: 'the flesh of his sons and daughters.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the second פסוק. It teaches that robbery hurts the victim's whole family, not only the victim himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in משלי speaks only of 'the life of its owners,' meaning the victim himself. The ירמיהו פסוק mentions sons and daughters. So it teaches that the robber is also considered to take the children's lives, because he took the food that feeds them.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, here is a source

phrases.english: And if you would say: his own life,
but not the life of his sons and daughters,
come and hear:
"the flesh of his sons and daughters."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 22 for the second פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second פסוק teaches that the robber is considered to take the lives of the victim's children too.

steps.title: The third פסוק: even if he pays, it is like killing
steps.stepSummary: We might think robbery is like murder only when the robber pays nothing. The פסוק in יואל calls חמס 'shedding innocent blood,' and חמס means taking something even while paying for it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say: this applies only where he does not pay, but where he pays, no. Come and hear: 'For the violence of the children of Judah, who shed innocent blood in their land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the third פסוק. It teaches that forcing someone to give up his property is like taking his life even if the taker pays for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Someone could think that paying for the item fixes the harm. The פסוק uses the word חמס, which describes taking something against the owner's will while paying for it, and it still calls this shedding innocent blood. So paying does not remove the seriousness.

keyTerms.meaning: These words apply, this rule is limited to
Where he does not give money

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that paying for something taken by force makes it acceptable. This פסוק teaches that it is still considered like shedding blood.
steps.whatToRemember: Each extra פסוק adds a detail. The second shows the robber harms the children too. The third shows that it is like killing even when the robber pays. The fourth פסוק, about שאול, is explained next.

phrases.english: And if you would say:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלָא יָהֵיב דְּמֵי,
phrases.english: this applies only where he does not pay money,
but where he does pay money, no,
come and hear:
"For the violence of the children of Judah,
phrases.notes: The point is the word חמס. It describes taking something by force even when you pay for it.

phrases.english: who shed innocent blood in their land."
phrases.notes: Some versions say 'your land' (the word in round brackets); the corrected wording in square brackets says 'their land,' which matches the פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא, הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּלָא יָהֵיב דְּמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues answering step 22, now for the third פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The third פסוק teaches that even taking by force with payment (חמס) is considered like shedding blood.

steps.title: Even indirect harm counts, as shown by the פסוק about שאול
steps.stepSummary: We might think robbery counts like murder only when done directly. The פסוק about שאול and the גבעונים teaches that even causing harm indirectly counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say this only applies when he does it directly with his own hands, but not when he only causes it indirectly, come and hear: 'For שאול and for his bloody house, because he killed the גבעונים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains what the last פסוק of רבי יוחנן adds. It shows that even indirect harm is treated as taking a life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 23 and 24 explained the first two extra פסוקים. Now the גמרא raises one more possible mistake: maybe only direct robbery is as bad as murder, and indirect damage (גרמא) is not. The פסוק about שאול and the גבעונים is brought to remove that mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: With one's own hands; doing something directly
Indirect causing; harm that happens because of what someone did, not by his own hands
Come and hear; introduces a source that proves the point
The people of גבעון, who served the Jewish people

phrases.english: And if you would say: these words apply
where he does it with his own hands,
but by indirect causing, no –
come and hear:
"For Shaul and for his bloody house,
because he put the Givonim to death";
phrases.notes: שמואל ב 21:1. The word in square brackets is added in the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא, הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּקָעָבֵיד בְּיָדַיִם, אֲבָל גְּרָמָא לָא – תָּא שְׁמַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third answer to the question of step 22, after steps 23 and 24 answered for the first two extra פסוקים.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The פסוק about שאול teaches that even indirect harm (גרמא) counts as taking a life.

steps.title: When did שאול ever kill the גבעונים?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where we ever find that שאול killed the גבעונים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where do we find that שאול killed the גבעונים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a puzzle in the פסוק. It is setting up the answer that will prove the point about indirect harm.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No story in תנ״ך tells of שאול killing the גבעונים. So the פסוק must mean something else, and the answer will show that it is talking about indirect harm.

keyTerms.meaning: Where do we find? Asks for a source or a story

phrases.english: And where do we find
that Shaul killed the Givonim?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי הֵיכָן מָצִינוּ שֶׁהָרַג שָׁאוּל אֶת הַגִּבְעוֹנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the plain meaning of the פסוק just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What act of killing the פסוק is talking about, since שאול never directly killed the גבעונים.

steps.title: Killing נוב cut off the גבעונים' food and water
steps.stepSummary: שאול killed the כהנים of נוב, who supplied the גבעונים with water and food. So the פסוק counts it as if he killed the גבעונים themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, because he killed נוב, the city of the כהנים, who used to supply them with water and food, the פסוק counts it against him as if he had killed them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that שאול harmed the גבעונים indirectly, and the פסוק still calls it killing them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שאול did not touch the גבעונים. But by destroying the people who fed them, he took away their way of living. The פסוק treats that as killing, so indirect robbery of someone's living is also like taking his life.

keyTerms.meaning: נוב, the city of the כהנים, which שאול destroyed
The פסוק counts it against him

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's statement is now fully explained. Robbing even a פרוטה is like taking a life. It harms the victim's children, it counts even if the robber paid, and it counts even when the harm is only indirect.

phrases.english: Rather, because he killed
Nov, the city of the kohanim,
phrases.notes: The story is in שמואל א 22.

phrases.english: who used to supply them with water and food,
phrases.notes: "Them" means the גבעונים.

phrases.english: the verse counts it against him as if he had killed them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁהָרַג נוֹב עִיר הַכֹּהֲנִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26 and completes the proof begun in step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: שאול killed the כהנים of נוב who fed the גבעונים, so he is counted as having killed the גבעונים.

steps.title: What may be bought from women, slaves and children
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה and brings a ברייתא. One may buy wool goods from women in יהודה and linen goods in the גליל, but not wine, oil or flour. One may not buy from slaves or children.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'But one may buy from women.' The Rabbis taught: One may buy from women wool goods in יהודה and linen goods in the גליל, but not wines, oils and flours. And not from slaves, and not from children.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and brings a ברייתא. It explains which goods may be bought from women.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה is about not buying from people who might be selling stolen goods. Women in each area were known to make and sell certain cloth goods, so buying those is fine. Wine, oil and flour are not things they usually sold, so we worry the items belong to the husband. Slaves and children usually own nothing of their own.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; introduces a ברייתא

phrases.english: But one may buy from women.
The Rabbis taught:
One may buy from women
wool goods in Yehudah
and linen goods in the Galil,
but not wines, oils and flours.

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא מִן הָעֲבָדִים, וְלֹא מִן הַתִּינוֹקוֹת.
phrases.english: And not from slaves, and not from children.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל לוֹקְחִין מִן הַנָּשִׁים. תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of רבי יוחנן and returns to the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Buy from women only goods they usually make and sell; not wine, oil or flour; never from slaves or children.

steps.title: אבא שאול: a woman may sell small amounts to buy a head covering
steps.stepSummary: אבא שאול says a woman may sell things worth up to four or five dinars to make a head covering.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבא שאול says: A woman may sell for four or five dinars, in order to make a head covering for herself.
steps.whatsHappening: אבא שאול adds that a woman may sell items for a small sum so she can buy a head covering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small sale like this is normal for a woman's own personal needs. So we assume her husband allows it, and the buyer need not worry that the items are stolen.

phrases.english: Abba Shaul says:
A woman may sell
for four or five dinars,
phrases.notes: The letters in square brackets are added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: in order to make a covering for her head.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further case where buying from a woman is allowed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman may sell up to four or five dinars' worth to make herself a head covering.

steps.title: If the seller says to hide it, buying is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: In all these cases, if the seller tells the buyer to hide the purchase, it is forbidden to buy.
steps.simpleTranslation: And in all of them, if they said to hide it, it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא gives one rule that covers every case above. A request to hide the item makes the sale forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when buying is normally allowed, asking to keep the sale hidden is a sign the seller has no permission. So the buyer must not buy.
steps.confusionAlert: This rule applies to every allowed case above, including אבא שאול's head covering. Permission to buy disappears once the seller asks for secrecy.

phrases.english: And all of them, where they said to hide it, it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sets a limit on all the permitted cases in steps 28 and 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Any sale where the seller asks the buyer to hide it is forbidden.

steps.title: Charity collectors may take only small donations
steps.stepSummary: גבאי צדקה may take a small item from them as charity, but not a large item.
steps.simpleTranslation: Charity collectors may take a small thing from them, but not a large thing.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now turns to charity collectors and says how much they may accept.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A small gift is something these givers are allowed to give on their own. A large gift may be more than they have permission to give, so the collectors must not accept it.
steps.confusionAlert: Here לוקחין means 'take' as a donation, not 'buy.' The collectors receive charity; they are not making a purchase.

phrases.english: Charity collectors may take from them
phrases.notes: "Them" refers to the people just listed, such as women.

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר מוּעָט, אֲבָל לֹא דָּבָר מְרוּבֶּה.
phrases.english: a small thing, but not a large thing.

steps.triggerLanguage: גַּבָּאֵי צְדָקָה לוֹקְחִין מֵהֶן דָּבָר מוּעָט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same concern to charity collectors receiving gifts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Charity collectors may accept small gifts but not large ones.

steps.title: From olive pressers buy large amounts, not small
steps.stepSummary: From olive pressers one may buy olives and oil in large measured amounts, but not in small amounts.
steps.simpleTranslation: And olive pressers: one may buy from them olives by measure and oil by measure, but not olives in small amounts and oil in small amounts.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא explains when one may buy from workers who press olives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A worker could easily sneak away a little olives or oil from the owner and sell it. A large amount is not something he would steal, so it is likely his own, and buying it is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Olive pressers, workers who press olives into oil
By measure; in a large, measured amount

phrases.english: And olive pressers – one may buy from them
olives by measure, and oil by measure.
phrases.notes: "By measure" here means a large amount, the kind sold by full measures.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל לֹא זֵיתִים בְּמוּעָט וְשֶׁמֶן בְּמוּעָט.
phrases.english: But not olives in small amounts and oil in small amounts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another type of seller to the ברייתא's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From olive pressers buy only large amounts of olives or oil, not small amounts.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: small amounts of olives from women in the Upper גליל
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows buying small amounts of olives from women in the Upper גליל. A man may be embarrassed to sell at his own door, so he gives olives to his wife to sell.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: One may buy small amounts of olives from women in the Upper גליל, because sometimes a man is embarrassed to sell at the entrance of his house, so he gives them to his wife and she sells.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל gives a special case where buying small amounts of olives from women is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a small sale might be from stolen goods. But in the Upper גליל it was common for a man to have his wife sell for him, out of embarrassment. So we assume she is selling with his permission.

keyTerms.meaning: The Upper גליל, the northern hill region

steps.whatToRemember: All these rules ask one question: is the seller likely to own the item or have permission to sell it? Local custom, the type of goods, the amount, and any request for secrecy all decide the answer.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One may buy small amounts of olives from women
in the Upper Galil,
because sometimes a man is embarrassed
to sell at the entrance of his house,
so he gives them to his wife and she sells.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an exception allowing small purchases of olives, unlike the rule for olive pressers in step 32.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In the Upper גליל one may buy small amounts of olives from women, since husbands commonly have their wives sell for them.

steps.title: רבינא accepts jewelry from the women of מחוזא
steps.stepSummary: רבינא came to מחוזא, and the women there threw chains and bracelets before him as צדקה. He accepted them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא came to מחוזא. The women of מחוזא came and threw chains and bracelets in front of him, and he accepted them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about רבינא accepting jewelry from women for צדקה. This story sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 31 taught that גבאי צדקה may take only a small item from women, because a large item may really belong to the husband. Here רבינא takes jewelry, which looks like a large item. That is the tension the next step will raise.

keyTerms.meaning: happened to come to / arrived at
מחוזא, a wealthy trading town in בבל

phrases.english: Ravina arrived at Bei Mechoza.
The women of Bei Mechoza came
and threw chains and bracelets before him,
and he accepted it from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a real-life case that tests the rule from step 31 about taking צדקה from women.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבינא accepted jewelry from women as צדקה.

steps.title: רבה תוספאה challenges רבינא from the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: רבה תוספאה asks how רבינא could accept jewelry, since a ברייתא says גבאי צדקה may take only small items from women.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה תוספאה said to רבינא: But a ברייתא teaches that charity collectors may accept a small item from women, but not a large item!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה תוספאה challenges רבינא's action. He quotes the ברייתא from step 31, which allows only small items.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Jewelry seems to be a large item. A large item may belong to the husband, so taking it could mean taking something the woman has no right to give. רבינא seems to be going against the ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: רבה תוספאה, an אמורא who lived in רבינא's time
but isn't it taught in a ברייתא?
a small item / a large item

phrases.english: Rabba Tosfa'a said to Ravina:
But isn't it taught: Charity collectors may accept from them
phrases.notes: "Them" means women. This is the ברייתא from step 31.

phrases.aramaic: דָּבָר מוּעָט, אֲבָל לֹא דָּבָר מְרוּבֶּה!
phrases.english: a small item, but not a large item!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבינא's action in step 34 using the ברייתא of step 31.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's accepting jewelry from the women
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא allows only small items from women. Jewelry is a large item, so accepting it should be forbidden.

steps.title: For the people of מחוזא, jewelry counts as small
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that for the wealthy people of מחוזא, chains and bracelets count as a small item.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: For the people of מחוזא, these are considered a small item.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers the challenge. He says that "small" depends on how wealthy the place is, and in מחוזא jewelry like this is small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא does not argue with the ברייתא. He explains it: a "small item" means something the husband would not mind. Since the people of מחוזא were very wealthy, their husbands would not mind, so the rule still allows it.
steps.whatToRemember: Whether an item counts as small or large is measured by local wealth. What is a big gift in one place may be a small one in a rich town like מחוזא.

phrases.english: He said to him: These,
for the people of Mechoza, are a small item.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: הָנֵי, לִבְנֵי מָחוֹזָא דָּבָר מוּעָט נִינְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 35.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the measure: "small" is measured by local wealth
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Jewelry is always a large item, so taking it breaks the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: In wealthy מחוזא, jewelry counts as small, so taking it is allowed.

steps.title: משנה: strands and threads from the launderer and carder
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that wool strands the launderer removes belong to him, but those the carder removes belong to the owner. A launderer may keep three threads, and more go to the owner. Black threads on a white garment all go to the launderer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Strands that the launderer removes are his, but strands the carder removes belong to the owner. A launderer takes three threads and they are his; more than that belong to the owner. If they were black threads on a white garment, he takes all of them and they are his.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on who keeps the small scraps that come off a garment while a craftsman works on it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The launderer removes only a few loose strands, which the owner does not care about, so they are his. The carder removes a lot, so the owner wants them back. Black threads on a white garment spoil its look, so the owner is happy to have them all removed and does not want them.

keyTerms.meaning: carder (who combs wool to prepare it)

steps.confusionAlert: Here בעל הבית does not mean a homeowner in general. It means the customer who owns the garment.

phrases.english: MISHNA: Strands that the launderer removes
belong to him,
but those the carder removes
belong to the owner.

phrases.aramaic: כּוֹבֵס נוֹטֵל שְׁלֹשָׁה חוּטִין – וְהֵן שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: A launderer takes three threads, and they are his;

phrases.aramaic: יָתֵר מִכֵּן – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת.
phrases.english: more than this, they belong to the owner.

phrases.aramaic: אִם הָיָה שָׁחוֹר עַל גַּבֵּי הַלָּבָן –
phrases.english: If it was black on white,
phrases.notes: He means black threads sewn into a white garment.

phrases.english: he takes all of them, and they are his.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה on a related idea: which leftovers the owner does not care about, so the worker may keep them.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Scraps the owner does not care about belong to the craftsman. Larger amounts the owner would want belong to the owner.

steps.title: משנה: tailor's leftovers and carpenter's shavings
steps.stepSummary: Leftover thread long enough to sew with, or a patch three by three, goes back to the owner. A carpenter keeps shavings from an adze, but chips from an ax go to the owner. If he works in the owner's home, even the small shavings go to the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: A tailor who left over enough thread to sew with, or a patch three by three: these belong to the owner. What a carpenter removes with an adze is his, but with an ax it belongs to the owner. And if he was working at the owner's place, even the shavings belong to the owner.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues with more craftsmen: the tailor and the carpenter. It applies the same idea of what the owner cares about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usable thread and a patch of three by three are worth something, so the owner wants them. An adze takes off only thin shavings, which the owner ignores, while an ax cuts off bigger chips that he wants. When the work is done on the owner's property, everything left there stays with the owner.

keyTerms.meaning: a patch or piece of cloth
adze, a tool that shaves off thin pieces
ax, a tool that cuts off larger chips

steps.whatToRemember: The whole משנה runs on one idea: if the owner would want the leftovers, they are his. If he would not care, the worker keeps them. Working on the owner's property gives everything to the owner.

phrases.english: A tailor who left over thread
enough to sew with,
and a patch that is three by three,
phrases.notes: Three fingerbreadths by three fingerbreadths.

phrases.english: these belong to the owner.
What a carpenter removes with an adze
belongs to him,
but what he removes with an ax belongs to the owner.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִם הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה אֵצֶל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת –
phrases.english: And if he was working at the owner's place,
even the shavings belong to the owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same משנה with the tailor and the carpenter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Usable leftovers and large chips go to the owner, and small shavings go to the carpenter. When the work is done at the owner's place, everything goes to the owner.

steps.title: ברייתא: buying strands from a launderer; he keeps two upper threads
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one may buy wool strands from a launderer, because they are his. It also says the launderer may keep the two upper threads.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: One may buy strands from a launderer, because they are his. A launderer takes the two upper threads, and they are his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins with a ברייתא about the launderer. This sets up the next discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא adds a practical rule. Since the strands belong to the launderer, buying them from him is not buying stolen goods. It also says "two upper threads," while the משנה said "three threads," a difference the גמרא will need to deal with.
steps.confusionAlert: Notice that the ברייתא says two threads, while the משנה says three. These are not the same number, so watch for how the גמרא explains the difference.

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Sages taught:
One may buy strands from a launderer,
because they are his.
A launderer takes the two upper threads,
and they are his.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: לוֹקְחִין מוֹכִין מִן הַכּוֹבֵס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא on the launderer's part of the משנה. It adds that one may buy from him, and its thread count differs from the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One may buy strands from a launderer, since they are his. He keeps the two upper threads.
